passage:
"Anjali, why are you awake? It's past midnight."
"Papa, is it because of my fees?"
Joseph sat on the edge of her bed. "Is what because of your fees?"
"You and Mama. Shouting. It started after the tuition fees went up. If I'd got the scholarship, you wouldn't fight."
"Mole, no."
"And last week, when Mama cried, that was after I broke the mixer."
"Anjali, listen. Mama and I are arguing about many things. Work, your grandmother's house, money. Grown-up things. Not you."
"But if I just did everything right..."
"Then we would still argue. You can't carry this. It isn't yours to fix."
She pulled the sheet up to her chin. "It feels like mine."
"I know. I'm sorry it does. Tomorrow Mama and I will both tell you this. Together."

qa.q: What did Anjali break before Mama cried?
qa.a: The mixer.

qa.q: Why does Anjali believe the fights are her fault?
qa.a: They began after the fees went up, so she links them to herself; believing she caused it also means she could fix it by doing everything right, which feels less helpless.

qa.q: What choice by Joseph helps Anjali most?
qa.a: Naming the real reasons as grown-up matters and planning to tell her together with Mama, so the message is clear and shared.

qa.q: How does Joseph feel when Anjali says "It feels like mine"?
qa.a: He is sorry and sad that his daughter has been carrying this, and wants to lift it off her rather than argue with her feelings.

grounding: A teenager blames herself for her parents' arguments, and her father explains that it is not hers to carry.

passage: When Samir got caught copying in the physics exam last month, I didn't sleep for two nights. The thing is, a week earlier he'd asked me to study with him and I'd said no, because I had cricket selection. So in my head it was simple: if I'd said yes, he'd have learned it, he wouldn't have copied, he wouldn't be suspended. My fault. I kept replaying it. I even went to the principal to say I should have helped him. The principal just looked at me kindly and said, "Kunal, Samir made a choice. You can care about him without owning it." I'm still thinking about that. I can be a good friend. I can't be the one who decides for him.

qa.q: Why did Kunal say no when Samir asked to study together?
qa.a: Because of cricket selection.

qa.q: Why did Kunal feel responsible for the suspension?
qa.a: Kunal linked one refusal to Samir's copying and imagined having the power to prevent it, which turned care for a friend into heavy guilt.

qa.q: What turning point helped Kunal see it differently?
qa.a: The principal's words, "Samir made a choice. You can care about him without owning it", which separated friendship from responsibility.

qa.q: How might Samir feel if he knew Kunal felt to blame?
qa.a: Samir might feel uncomfortable or sorry, since the copying was his own decision, and may not want his friend carrying it.

grounding: A teenager takes the blame for a friend's decision to copy, until seeing that the choice was the friend's.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Sunaina, Grade 9, 20 November
Vikas asked to see me after assembly. His class teacher had mentioned he'd gone quiet and his marks were slipping, and today he told me why: his parents have been arguing a lot, and he believes it is because of him. "If I didn't need so much, if I got better marks, they'd be okay." He listed his "mistakes" in detail. He looked exhausted. I asked if he feels safe at home; he said yes, it's the shouting and the silence afterwards. I told him clearly that adults' arguments are the adults' responsibility, not his. What I did next: with his agreement, I called his mother this afternoon, and the three of us will meet on Friday. I'll check in with Vikas every day this week.

qa.q: When will Sunaina, Vikas and his mother meet?
qa.a: On Friday.

qa.q: Why might Vikas believe his parents' arguments are his fault?
qa.a: If the fights are his doing, he could stop them by needing less and scoring more; that feels less helpless than accepting he can't control them, but it leaves him exhausted with guilt.

qa.q: What choice by Sunaina helps lift the weight from Vikas?
qa.a: Saying plainly that the arguments are the adults' responsibility, checking he is safe, and bringing his mother into a meeting so the message comes from home too.

qa.q: How might Vikas's mother react to the counsellor's call?
qa.a: She may be shocked and sad to learn her son blames himself, and glad of the chance to tell him directly that it isn't his fault.

grounding: A counsellor notes a teenager who blames himself for his parents' fights and responds the same day.

passage:
Thursday night
Farhan got suspended for a week for bunking the maths exam. On Tuesday he'd asked me to tell Ma'am he was sick, and I said no. So it's my fault. If I'd covered for him he wouldn't be in trouble, and his Ammi wouldn't have cried at the school gate. I couldn't eat dinner.
Told Amma at bedtime. I thought she'd say, "Yes, you should have helped." Instead she put her phone down and hugged me. She said, "Ganga, you didn't choose to skip the exam. Farhan did. Saying no to lying was right." She said I can still be a good friend: message him, share my notes.
I still feel heavy. But lighter than at dinner.
Sending him the notes tomorrow.

qa.q: Why was Farhan suspended?
qa.a: Farhan got suspended for a week for bunking the maths exam.

qa.q: Why does Ganga feel it's all Ganga's fault?
qa.a: Because Ganga refused to cover for Farhan, that 'no' seems to have caused the suspension and his Ammi's tears; taking on that much control turns into guilt.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did Ganga decide after it?
qa.a: Amma saying that Farhan chose to skip and that refusing to lie was right; Ganga decided to stay a good friend by sending the notes instead of carrying the blame.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel when Ganga's notes arrive?
qa.a: Farhan might feel relieved that his friend isn't angry or distant, and supported while catching up on a week of missed classes.

grounding: A teenager blames themselves for a friend's choice to skip an exam until a parent helps separate responsibility.

passage: Last winter in Gangtok, my parents fought almost every night. About the shop, about my uncle, about everything. I lay in bed listening and made a list in my head of what I'd done wrong that day. Came home late. Got a C in chemistry. Forgot to buy milk. I was sure if I were better, they'd stop. So I tried to be perfect. I did the dishes before anyone asked. I studied till midnight. And still they fought. That made it worse; I thought I wasn't trying hard enough. It was Sangeeta aunty, our neighbour, who found me crying on the stairs one evening. I told her. She sat with me and said, "Pema, beti, grown-ups' fights are grown-ups' business. It is not your fault." She walked me home and spoke to my mother that night. I didn't believe her fully then. I'm starting to.

qa.q: What did Pema list in bed each night?
qa.a: What Pema had done wrong that day, like coming home late, getting a C in chemistry, and forgetting to buy milk.

qa.q: Why did Pema feel it was Pema's fault that the parents fought?
qa.a: Pema felt guilty and anxious, believing that being better would stop the fights; this sense of too much control made every fight feel personal.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta aunty do that helped?
qa.a: She listened, told Pema clearly it wasn't Pema's fault, and spoke to Pema's mother that same night.

qa.q: How might Pema's mother feel hearing from Sangeeta aunty?
qa.a: Pema's mother might feel shocked and sad that Pema carried that guilt, and want to reassure Pema.

grounding: It shows a teenager who blames herself for her parents' conflict, where too much perceived control turns into guilt.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Thursday

Hafsa came to me after the last bell, very upset. Her close friend Meenu has been skipping school for the past week and spending the day at the bus stand with older boys. Hafsa kept saying, "It's my fault, sir. I should have stopped her. I knew on Monday." She has not been sleeping well, she said, and she missed her own maths test to look for Meenu.

I told Hafsa that telling me was exactly the right thing, and that Meenu's choices are Meenu's, not hers. She cried, and said she still felt responsible. I did not argue; I sat with her until she was calmer.

Next steps: I informed Meenu's class teacher and the school counsellor today, and they are calling Meenu's parents this evening. I've asked Hafsa to meet the counsellor tomorrow too.

— Sahil

qa.q: What did Hafsa miss to look for Meenu?
qa.a: Her own maths test.

qa.q: Why does Hafsa believe Meenu's skipping is her fault?
qa.a: Hafsa feels guilty and responsible because she knew on Monday, so she thinks she should have been able to stop Meenu, as if she controls her friend's choices.

qa.q: What did Sahil do well in handling Hafsa's worry?
qa.a: Sahil listened, told Hafsa it was right to share and that Meenu's choices aren't hers, informed the counsellor and Meenu's class teacher the same day, and set up support for Hafsa.

qa.q: How might Meenu's parents feel when the school calls them?
qa.a: They may feel worried and shocked, but glad the school found out quickly so they can help Meenu.

grounding: It shows, through a teacher's note, a teenager who blames herself for a friend's bad choices, turning too much sense of control into guilt.

passage:
Wednesday night

Shreya got caught copying in the physics test today. Madam took her paper and sent her to the principal. Shreya cried in the corridor, and all I could think was: it's my fault.

I lent her my notes on Monday. She said she'd study from them. If I'd made her study with me, she wouldn't have needed to copy. If I'd sat next to her. If I'd noticed she was stressed. I kept going round and round in my head.

At dinner Mumma asked why I wasn't eating. I told her. She said, "Mehak, you lent notes to help. Shreya chose what she did." I said yes, but I still feel sick.

Maybe she's right. It feels like I should have been able to stop it. Shreya won't answer my messages.

Going to sleep. Or trying.

— Mehak

qa.q: What did Mehak lend Shreya on Monday?
qa.a: Mehak's notes.

qa.q: Why does Mehak feel it's Mehak's fault that Shreya copied?
qa.a: Mehak feels guilty and sick, imagining many ways Shreya could have been stopped, as if Mehak had control over Shreya's choice.

qa.q: What might help Mehak with this guilt?
qa.a: Talking more with Mumma or a school counsellor, and reminding Mehak that lending notes was kind and Shreya made her own choice.

qa.q: How might Shreya be feeling as she ignores Mehak's messages?
qa.a: Shreya may feel ashamed and upset about being caught, not wanting to talk to anyone yet.

grounding: It shows a teenager who blames themselves for a friend's bad choice, where too much sense of control becomes guilt.

passage:
In Karad, Chandrika, sixteen, sat on the steps outside the temple long after the evening aarti.
Her friend Eshaan had been caught bunking school to hang around the bus stand with older boys. His father had been called in.
Chandrika kept going over it. She had seen him skip on Monday and hadn't said anything. On Tuesday she'd been too busy with her project to walk home with him. If she had, maybe he wouldn't have gone.
“It's my fault,” she told her mother at dinner.
Her mother put down the ladle. “Did you tell him to bunk?”
“No.”
“Did you take him to the bus stand?”
“No, but…”
“Then it's his choice. You can be sad for him. You can talk to him. But you can't carry what he chose, beta.”
Chandrika nodded slowly, but the heavy feeling in her chest stayed a while longer.

qa.q: Where had Eshaan been hanging around when he bunked school?
qa.a: He had been hanging around the bus stand with older boys.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika feel it was her fault?
qa.a: She felt guilty and over-responsible, thinking that if she had spoken up or walked home with him, he wouldn't have gone.

qa.q: What did Chandrika's mother help her see?
qa.a: That Eshaan's choice was his own; Chandrika can care and talk to him but doesn't have to carry the blame.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel if he knew Chandrika blamed herself?
qa.a: Eshaan might feel surprised and a bit guilty himself, since it was his own decision to bunk.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager blaming herself for a friend's bad choices, with too much perceived control turning into guilt.

passage:
In Melbourne, Chidi, fifteen, sat in the school library, not reading. His friend Tuan had been caught copying answers in the maths exam and was suspended for two days.
Chidi kept replaying it. Last week Tuan had asked to see his homework, and Chidi had said yes. If he'd said no, maybe Tuan wouldn't have thought copying was fine. Maybe it had started with him.
When the librarian, Ms Patel, asked if he was okay, he blurted, “It's my fault Tuan cheated.”
She sat down. “Did you give him your exam answers?”
“No. Just homework, once.”
“Did you tell him to copy?”
“No.”
“Then you're carrying something that isn't yours. You can be a good friend. You can tell him what you think. But you're not in charge of his choices.”
Chidi let out a long breath. It was hard to believe.

qa.q: How long was Tuan suspended?
qa.a: Tuan was suspended for two days.

qa.q: Why does Chidi believe it's his fault Tuan cheated?
qa.a: He feels guilty and over-responsible, linking one shared homework to Tuan's decision to copy in the exam.

qa.q: What did Ms Patel do that could help Chidi?
qa.a: She asked simple questions that separated Chidi's actions from Tuan's choices and told him he isn't in charge of them.

qa.q: How might Tuan feel about Chidi blaming himself?
qa.a: Tuan might feel surprised and uncomfortable, since the choice to copy was Tuan's alone.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager blaming himself for a friend's cheating, with too much perceived control turning into guilt.

passage:
The school counsellor's room smelled of old files and phenyl. Simran sat on the edge of the chair, twisting her dupatta.
"Anand skipped the board practical," she said. "He went to the arcade with those Class 12 boys. Now he might have to repeat."
"And you're here because...?" asked Mrs Pinto.
"Because it's my fault. He told me on Monday he was thinking of skipping. I said, 'Don't be stupid,' and changed the topic. I should have argued more. Or told his mother. Or gone with him to the lab."
"Did you tell him to skip?"
"No, but—"
"Did you take him to the arcade?"
"No."
"So whose choice was it?"
Simran stared at her hands. "His. But I could have stopped it." Her eyes were wet. "I always think I could have stopped things."

qa.q: Where did Anand go instead of the board practical?
qa.a: He went to the arcade with some Class 12 boys.

qa.q: Why does Simran feel that Anand's skipping is her fault?
qa.a: She feels guilty because she believes she could have argued more or told his mother, as if his choice was hers to control.

qa.q: How is Mrs Pinto helping Simran, and what could come next?
qa.a: Mrs Pinto asks simple questions that separate Simran's actions from Anand's choice; next she could help Simran see what a good friend can and cannot control.

qa.q: How might Anand see his own choice?
qa.a: Anand probably sees skipping as his own decision with the older boys and may not even know Simran feels responsible.

grounding: It shows a teenager blaming herself for a friend's bad choice, as too strong a sense of control turns into guilt.

passage:
Dear Vinita didi,
You said I could write when things get bad at home. They're bad.
Mummy and Papa fought again last night, loud, about money and about Dadi's visit. It started when I asked for money for the school trip. So I keep thinking, if I hadn't asked, it wouldn't have happened.
Last month it started after I got a low maths mark. Before that, I think it was because I left the geyser on. It feels like every fight starts with something I did. I've started staying in my room and not asking for anything, just in case.
I know you'll say it's not my fault. But I'm the one they fight about, aren't I?
Please write back soon. Or call on Sunday. I'll keep my phone on.
Vikas

qa.q: What did Vikas ask for just before last night's fight?
qa.a: Vikas asked for money for the school trip.

qa.q: How does Vikas feel about the fights at home?
qa.a: Vikas feels guilty and anxious, believing every fight starts with something Vikas did, so hiding in the room and not asking for anything feels safer.

qa.q: What could Vinita didi do after reading this letter?
qa.a: Vinita didi could call Vikas on Sunday, gently explain that parents' fights come from their own worries, not a child's small actions, and suggest talking to a trusted adult or school counsellor.

qa.q: How might Vikas's parents feel if they knew about this letter?
qa.a: They would likely feel sad and shaken to learn that Vikas feels to blame for their fights, and might want to reassure Vikas directly.

grounding: It shows a teenager blaming themselves for family conflict, as too much perceived control turns into guilt and withdrawal.

"You want to know why I've been so quiet, Ojas? Okay. It's Priya. You know she quit the basketball team last week?
I'm Mahima, and I think it's my fault. She told me in the changing room that she felt left out, and I said, 'Just give it time.' That's all I said. I didn't talk to the coach. I didn't stay back with her after practice. Then she quit.
I keep replaying it. If I'd said something better. If I'd sat with her at lunch. If I'd noticed earlier. Every version, I'm the one who could have fixed it.
My mum says Priya made her own decision, and that her parents were also moving her to tuition. But it doesn't feel like that. It feels like I dropped her.
I know it sounds dramatic. It just sits on my chest all the time."

passage:
Saturday, three days before Christmas. Jaya heard her parents arguing about the electricity bill while the plastic tree blinked in the corner. She went to her room and thought: if I hadn't asked for the new school shoes, there'd be money. She lay awake counting everything she had asked for that year.
Tuesday. Zubin texted that he'd skipped tuition again to hang out at the station. Jaya stared at the message. I should've made him come with me. I should've said something last week. She apologised to him twice, though he hadn't asked.
Christmas Day. Her mother hugged her at breakfast and said the bill was sorted. Jaya smiled, but inside she was already listing what she'd done wrong this time, as if every quarrel and every choice in her world had passed through her hands first.

qa.q: What were Jaya's parents arguing about?
qa.a: They were arguing about the electricity bill.

qa.q: What is Jaya feeling when she apologises to Zubin twice?
qa.a: She feels guilty and anxious, because she believes she should have stopped him skipping tuition, as if his choices were hers to control.

qa.q: What could help Jaya when she starts listing her mistakes?
qa.a: She could write down who actually made each choice, such as her parents and Zubin, and talk the list through with a trusted adult like her mother or a school counsellor.

qa.q: If you were Zubin, how might you feel receiving Jaya's apologies?
qa.a: Zubin might feel puzzled or even uncomfortable, since he made the choice to skip tuition himself and never asked her to say sorry.

grounding: A teenager blames herself for her parents' argument and a friend's choices, showing how too much felt control becomes guilt.
